interactions.label: Which enzyme does HIV use to convert its RNA genome into DNA inside the host cel

params.question: Which enzyme does HIV use to convert its RNA genome into DNA inside the host cell?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DNA polymerase replicates the host cell's own DNA. HIV uses a viral enzyme called reverse transcriptase, which is unique to retroviruses and a key drug target.
Correct. Reverse transcriptase converts viral single-stranded RNA into double-stranded DNA, a defining feature of retroviruses. Its high error rate (~1 mutation per cycle) drives drug resistance.
Integrase is another HIV enzyme, but its role is to insert the newly formed viral DNA into the host chromosome — it does not perform the RNA-to-DNA conversion.
Protease cleaves large viral polyproteins into functional units during viral maturation. The RNA-to-DNA conversion is carried out by reverse transcriptase.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: HIV encodes its genome as RNA. Reverse transcriptase converts this RNA into DNA, which can then be integrated into the host chromosome.
Reverse transcriptase is the hallmark enzyme of retroviruses and the target of several antiretroviral drugs including tenofovir and lamivudine.

interactions.label: Why does the integration of proviral DNA into the host chromosome make complete

params.question: Why does the integration of proviral DNA into the host chromosome make complete eradication of HIV particularly difficult?

answers.text: It prevents the immune system from producing antibodies against HIV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The body does produce anti-HIV antibodies (detected by ELISA). The challenge is not antibody production but the virus hiding within host DNA where drugs cannot reach it.

answers.text: It causes the host cell to become resistant to all antiretroviral drugs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antiretroviral drugs act on viral enzymes, not on host cells. The difficulty lies in the proviral DNA remaining silent within the host genome, reactivating when the cell activates.

answers.text: It creates a latent reservoir in host chromosomes that persists beyond the reach of antiretroviral therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host chromosome. These latently infected cells harbour the provirus indefinitely. When they activate, the viral protein tat drives rapid replication — restarting the infection cycle.

answers.text: It accelerates viral mutation by activating host cell DNA repair mechanisms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral mutation is driven by the error-prone reverse transcriptase, not by host DNA repair. The latent reservoir's significance is that it shelters the virus from ART inside the host genome.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host chromosome, creating latently infected cells. These cells can reactivate at any time, which is why ART must be lifelong.
The latent reservoir is the fundamental barrier to an HIV cure. Even after years of undetectable viral load on ART, stopping treatment allows reactivation from these integrated proviral DNA copies.

params.question: A patient with a CD4 count of 130 cells/μL was started on anti-tuberculosis treatment, followed by antiretroviral therapy two weeks later. Five weeks after starting ART, he develops worsening fever and enlarging lymph nodes despite good adherence. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: Drug-resistant tuberculosis requiring a change in the anti-TB regimen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Drug resistance typically presents as failure to improve on treatment or microbiological non-conversion, not as paradoxical worsening after initial improvement once ART is added.

Correct. IRIS occurs 4–8 weeks after starting ART when the recovering immune system mounts vigorous inflammation against an existing pathogen (here, TB). This is not treatment failure — it reflects immune recovery.
While new infections are possible, the characteristic timeline (worsening 4–8 weeks after ART initiation in a patient already being treated for TB) points strongly to IRIS, not a new pathogen.

answers.text: Hepatotoxicity from the combination of anti-TB and antiretroviral drugs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hepatotoxicity would present with jaundice, elevated transaminases, and gastrointestinal symptoms — not worsening lymphadenopathy. The clinical picture here fits the paradoxical inflammation of IRIS.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: When immunity recovers after starting ART, it can mount vigorous inflammation against pathogens already present (like TB). This immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome appears 4–8 weeks after ART initiation and is not treatment failure.
IRIS is a recognised complication when ART is started during active infection. The key teaching point: apparent worsening after starting ART does not always mean the treatment is failing.

params.question: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a known HIV-positive patient 48 hours ago. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Reassure and retest after 3 months, as the 72-hour window for prophylaxis has passed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 72-hour window has NOT passed — only 48 hours have elapsed. Post-exposure prophylaxis is still indicated and should be started immediately.

answers.text: Start daily tenofovir and emtricitabine as pre-exposure prophylaxis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PrEP (tenofovir + emtricitabine) is for HIV-negative individuals at ongoing risk BEFORE exposure. After a needlestick, the correct intervention is post-exposure prophylaxis with a three-drug regimen.

answers.text: Start tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir for 28 days as post-exposure prophylaxis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PEP must begin within 72 hours of exposure. The recommended regimen is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD) — the same combination used as India's first-line ART — taken for 28 days.

answers.text: Obtain an HIV RNA test first and start treatment only if positive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Waiting for test results would waste the critical 72-hour window. PEP is started empirically after significant exposure; baseline testing is done simultaneously but does not delay prophylaxis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review: After a significant HIV exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis (TDF + 3TC + DTG for 28 days) must be started within 72 hours. Do not wait for test results — start prophylaxis and test simultaneously.
PEP within 72 hours with TDF + 3TC + DTG for 28 days is the standard of care after occupational HIV exposure. The same TLD regimen is India's preferred first-line ART.
